1.pericope_label: Again, David gathered together all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. And David arose, and went with all the people that were with him from Baale of Judah, to bring up from thence the ark of God, whose name is called by the name of the Lord of hosts that dwelleth between the cherubims. And they set the ark of God upon a new cart, and brought it out of the house of Abinadab that was in Gibeah: and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drave the new cart. And they brought it out of the house of Abinadab which was at Gibeah, accompanying the ark of God: and Ahio went before the ark. And David and all the house of Israel played before the Lord on all manner of instruments made of fir wood, even on harps, and on psalteries, and on timbrels, and on cornets, and on cymbals.

schools.summary: Delitzsch defends Baale-Jehudah as a place name against the ancient versions and Luther, who took it appellatively as the rulers or citizens of Judah, since the following word thence is otherwise unintelligible; he puts the ark's stay in Abinadab's house at about seventy years and uses the span to explain how Uzzah and Ahio can still be called his sons. He also finds the text corrupt at the music: all manner of woods of cypress can only mean instruments of cypress wood, and even then the expression would be very strange, so he takes the Chronicles reading, with all their might and with songs, for the original from which ours has sprung, noting that the Greek combines the two. Ellicott identifies Baale with Kirjath-jearim, holds that either from should be read to or the historian has passed over the outward journey, and re-translates the clause about the name as which is called by the name, the name of Jehovah of hosts. On the cart he is gentlest of all, that it was doubtless meant as a mark of respect and that the exact requirements may easily have passed out of mind after so long a neglect.

Gill notes that the Greek gives seventy thousand for the muster where the Targum and Syriac keep the Hebrew's thirty. On the cart he finds it strange that so many priests and Levites, and David so versed in the law, did not consult it, and refuses the Philistine precedent as an excuse, since those were ignorant heathen with no proper persons to bear the ark, and so might be dispensed with.

Clarke identifies Baale with Kirjath-jearim and suspects a scribal doubling in the clause about the name, the second occurrence probably to be read there, so that the sense is that there the name of the Lord of hosts was invoked. On the cart he allows that a new one was used through respect but is the only witness to draw the consequence directly, that the neglect of the proper carriage was the cause of Uzzah's death. Wesley states the principle behind the Philistine precedent exactly: God might wink at the Philistines because they were ignorant of his laws, and yet be angry with Israel for the same act, because they knew or might have known; he adds that their joy made them inconsiderate.

Henry observes that nothing has been heard of the ark since Kirjath-jearim but the once when Saul called for it, and draws from its long obscurity that perpetual visibility is no mark of the true church, God being present with his people even when they want the outward tokens. On the cart his formulation is the memorable one, that Philistines may cart the ark with impunity but Israelites do so at their peril, and old or new it was not what God appointed; he wonders how so wise and good a man came to be guilty of such an oversight and charitably hopes it was because he was so intent upon the substance of the service that he forgot the circumstance. On the rejoicing he holds that as secret worship is better the more secret it is, so public worship is better the more public, though public joy must always be as before the Lord and not degenerate into what is carnal, and he passes on the suggestion that David wrote the sixty-eighth psalm for the occasion.

6.pericope_label: And when they came to Nachon’s threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God, and took hold of it; for the oxen shook it. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God. And David was displeased, because the Lord had made a breach upon Uzzah: and he called the name of the place Perez–uzzah to this day. And David was afraid of the Lord that day, and said, How shall the ark of the Lord come to me? So David would not remove the ark of the Lord unto him into the city of David: but David carried it aside into the house of Obed–edom the Gittite. And the ark of the Lord continued in the house of Obed–edom the Gittite three months: and the Lord blessed Obed–edom, and all his household.

schools.summary: Delitzsch says the oxen slipped, renders the threshingfloor's name as the floor of the stroke and supposes it came from the incident rather than an owner. Ellicott offers a suggestion nobody else makes, that the oxen turned aside to snatch the scattered grain of the floor, says the place is entirely unknown, and holds that what seems an exceedingly severe penalty for a well-meaning though unlawful act was on reflection a necessary manifestation of displeasure, involving not only a breach of the letter, of which David was equally guilty, but a disposition to profane familiarity with sacred things. On Uzzah's own case he stops carefully short: judgments of this kind were temporal and give no indication in themselves of the offender's treatment beyond the grave. He defends David's anger as vexation at an untoward interruption rather than anger with God, and takes the fear that followed as the intended effect, producing the awe in which they had been deficient.
Gill takes Nachon and the Chidon of the parallel for two names of one man or place.

Clarke goes further than any other witness on Uzzah's eternal state: he sinned through ignorance and precipitancy, having no time to reflect when the oxen stumbled, and no man can doubt of his eternal safety, since he committed a sin unto death but the mercy of God was doubtless extended to his soul. He also draws the rule from Obed-edom, that whoever entertains God's messengers or consecrates his house to his service will infallibly be blessed. Wesley argues the severity from the general good: men are improper judges of God's actions, and it is reasonable he should make examples against sins seemingly small, so there is more of mercy than of justice in such acts, the justice confined to one person while the benefit is common to mankind in all future ages. He makes David's displeasure grief rather than anger, and sets Obed-edom's courage against the general fear, since he knew what slaughter the ark had made and had seen Uzzah struck dead, yet opened his doors, knowing it a savour of death only to those who treated it ill.

Henry reports the critics divided on what the oxen did, and gives several reasons for the severity: the touching was forbidden on pain of death, so God would show how he might have dealt with our first parents; he saw the presumption of Uzzah's heart, familiarity even with what is most awful being apt to breed contempt; and a good intention will not justify a bad action, since it will not suffice to say of what is ill done that it was well meant. On David he is severe where the others excuse: it is not said David was angry because Uzzah had affronted God but because God had made a breach upon Uzzah, the very word used of God's own anger, so David did not then act like a man after God's own heart, and when we lie under God's anger we must keep under our own.

12.pericope_label: And it was told king David, saying, The Lord hath blessed the house of Obed–edom, and all that pertaineth unto him, because of the ark of God. So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed–edom into the city of David with gladness. And it was so, that when they that bare the ark of the Lord had gone six paces, he sacrificed oxen and fatlings. And David danced before the Lord with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod. So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the Lord with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet. And as the ark of the Lord came into the city of David, Michal Saul’s daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the Lord; and she despised him in her heart. And they brought in the ark of the Lord, and set it in his place, in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it: and David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord. And as soon as David had made an end of offering burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts. And he dealt among all the people, even among the whole multitude of Israel, as well to the women as men, to every one a cake of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine. So all the people departed every one to his house.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that David no longer presumed to violate the law and took care the ark should be borne by the proper persons, and corrects a common notion about the sacrifices: it is unnecessary to suppose offerings were made at every six steps, for although possible it is not recorded, David sacrificing when the removal had been successfully begun and again when the journey was done. On the dancing he observes that such religious dances were usually performed by women only, so the king by joining marked his sense of the occasion. On the linen ephod he disputes the usual assumption at length, since the ephod was not prescribed as part of the priestly dress at all, the high priest's being quite a different thing, it was worn by others such as Samuel, it is elsewhere connected with idolatrous worship, and the high priest's was of one material where the ephods of Samuel and David were of another: it was simply a garment worn by anyone engaged in religious service. Delitzsch by contrast calls it strictly a priestly costume denoting the priestly character of the wearer, and has David wear it as head of the priestly nation; he also observes that Michal is called the daughter of Saul here and not the wife of David, because on this occasion she showed her father's disposition rather than her husband's.

Gill notes that David had seen the former mistake and ordered the Levites to bear the ark on their shoulders with the staves. On the dancing he reports that the Targum renders it praised before the Lord with all his might, that the Greek and Syriac agree, and that Castel approved this since it nowhere appears to have been a custom to dance before the ark, though he grants that a later writer shows dancing to be the proper sense and himself takes it of leaping and skipping as a lamb.

Clarke is the one witness openly uncomfortable with the dancing: it is a religious ceremony among the Hindoos, who consider it an act of devotion to their idols, and it is evident to him that David considered it so; what connection dancing can have with devotion he cannot tell, though he allows that unpremeditated and involuntary skipping may be the effect of sudden mental elation. On Michal he notes what she did not do, making no outward reproach but keeping her mind to herself. Wesley normalises the dancing as thankfulness expressed by outward carriage after the manner of those times, keeps the priestly sense of the ephod but turns it to David's humility, that he laid by his royal robes to declare that though king he willingly owned himself the Lord's minister and servant, and has Michal despise him as of a base and mean spirit who knew not how to carry himself with the majesty that became his place.

20.pericope_label: Then David returned to bless his household. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, How glorious was the king of Israel to day, who uncovered himself to day in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself! And David said unto Michal, It was before the Lord, which chose me before thy father, and before all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the Lord, over Israel: therefore will I play before the Lord. And I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight: and of the maidservants which thou hast spoken of, of them shall I be had in honour. Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains that the blessing was for those of the household whom eastern custom barred from the ceremonies, calls Michal's speech cutting irony, and notes that the whole scene is omitted from Chronicles. On David's reply he reads a past where our version has a future, rather, have I danced, and observes that the Greek, not understanding the next clause, altered base in mine own sight to in thine eyes, when the meaning is that where Michal charged him with making himself base before the maidservants, who were no fit judges, David was ready to abase himself in his own eyes for God's honour. On Michal's barrenness he supposes the long separation during David's outlawry, when she was married to a man deeply attached to her, had estranged them, so that when their different spirit came out David determined on no further intercourse. Delitzsch renders the verb as a past in the same way, notes that the reminder of God's choosing David before her father humbles the pride of the king's daughter, and makes the childlessness God's humbling of her for her pride.

Gill keeps the future, that if this is to be vile he will endeavour to be viler still, and offers a third reason for the childlessness, from Abarbinel, that it was so ordered in providence that the seed of David and of Saul might not be mixed; he disposes of the children she is elsewhere said to have brought up as adopted or another woman's.

Clarke makes the barrenness David's doing, that probably he never more took her to his bed, while allowing that God might have subjected her to a barrenness counted in that country both a misfortune and a reproach. He draws the chapter's closing lesson: Michal formed her judgment without reason and meddled with what she did not understand, and we should be careful how we attribute actions whose reasons we cannot comprehend to motives that seem unjustifiable, since rash judgments are doubly pernicious, hurting those who form them and those of whom they are formed. Wesley makes the childlessness a punishment for her proud and petulant carriage, and repeats Henry's doctrine almost word for word, that the more we are vilified for well doing the more resolute we should be.

Henry turns the blessing of the household into a rule, that public performances do not excuse a man from family worship, and observes that David, though he had prophets and priests for chaplains, blessed his household himself, since it is angels' work to worship God and can be no disparagement to the greatest of men; even the palaces of princes, he adds, are not exempt from domestic troubles. On Michal he is careful with the facts: it was not her covetousness but her pride that made her fret, and she represented his conduct as lewd and immodest, but we have no reason to think it was true, David no doubt observing decorum and governing his zeal with discretion, and it is common for those who reproach religion to put false colours upon it. He notices too that her contempt began in the heart and only afterwards reached the tongue, and that the exercises of religion appear very mean to those who have little religion themselves.
